### 1.1-1.3 Problem Analysis

The issue is with **named annotation message filtering** in PyBryt. Specifically:

**Technical Details:**
- **Classes/Methods:** `pybryt.Value`, `pybryt.ReferenceImplementation`, message filtering logic
- **Parameters:** `name`, `success_message`, `failure_message` 
- **Variables:** `max_ref`, test lists, student implementation

**Problem Statement:**
When a group of named annotations (same `name` parameter) contains both:
- A `success_message` but no `failure_message` 
- At least one unsatisfied annotation

The system incorrectly shows the success message even though the reference group is registered as not satisfied. According to the expected behavior, **no message should be shown** in this scenario.

### 1.4 Steps to Reproduce
1. Create multiple `pybryt.Value` objects with the same `name` and a `success_message` but no `failure_message`
2. Group them into a `ReferenceImplementation`
3. Implement a student solution that satisfies some but not all of these named annotations
4. Run the check - observe that success message is shown despite the group being unsatisfied

### 1.5 Best Practices for Testing/Fixing
- Understand existing message filtering logic for named annotations
- Ensure changes don't break existing functionality
- Test edge cases (mixed success/failure messages, all satisfied, all unsatisfied)
- Make minimal, focused changes

![PyBrytGoals](https://github.com/microsoft/pybryt/blob/main/images/pybryt-goals.PNG "PyBryt Goals") 23 - The PyBryt Library will work existing auto grading solution such as [Otter Grader](https://pypi.org/project/otter-grader/), [OkPy](https://pypi.org/project/okpy/) or [Autolab](https://pypi.org/project/autolab/). 24 25 ## Features 26 27 Educators and Institutions can leverage the PyBryt Library to integrate auto assessment and reference models to hands on labs and assessments. 28 29 - Educators do not have to enforce the structure of the solution; 30 - Learner practice the design process,code design and implemented solution; 31 - Meaningful & pedagogical feedback to the learners; 32 - Analysis of complexity within the learners solution; 33 - Plagiarism detection and support for reference solutions; 34 - Easy integration into existing organizational or institutional grading infrastructure. 35 36 ## Getting Started 37 38 See the [Getting Started](https://microsoft.github.io/pybryt/html/getting_started.html) page on the pybryt documentation for steps to install and use pybryt for the first time. You can also check the [Microsoft Learn interactive module on pybryt](http://aka.ms/pybrytlearn) to learn how to use the library. 39 40 ## Testing 41 42 To run the demos, all demos are located in the demo folder. 43 44 First install PyBryt with `pip`: 45 46 ``` 47 pip install pybryt 48 ``` 49 50 Simply launch the `index.ipynb` notebook in each of the directories under `demo` from Jupyter Notebook, which demonstrates the process of using PyBryt to assess student submissions. 51 52 ## Technical Report 53 54 We continuously interact with computerized systems to achieve goals and perform tasks in our personal and professional lives. Therefore, the ability to program such systems is a skill needed by everyone. Consequently, computational thinking skills are essential for everyone, which creates a challenge for the educational system to teach these skills at scale and allow students to practice these skills. To address this challenge, we present a novel approach to providing formative feedback to students on programming assignments. Our approach uses dynamic evaluation to trace intermediate results generated by student's code and compares them to the reference implementation provided by their teachers. We have implemented this method as a Python library and demonstrate its use to give students relevant feedback on their work while allowing teachers to challenge their students' computational thinking skills.
